q: Solve \( x^2-6x+13=0 \) and verify the root \( x=3+2i \).
c:
Solution

Complete the square:

\[\begin{aligned}x^2-6x+13&=0\\x^2-6x+9&=-4\\(x-3)^2&=-4\\x-3&=\pm 2i\\x&=3\pm 2i.\end{aligned}\]


Substitute \( x=3+2i \):

\[\begin{aligned}(3+2i)^2-6(3+2i)+13&= 9+12i+4i^2-18-12i+13\\&= 9-4-18+13=0.\end{aligned}\]


The root is verified.

Answer   \(x=3\pm 2i\)

Solution

Use \( x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a} \) with \( a=3 \), \( b=2 \), \( c=1 \).

\[\begin{aligned}x&=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-12}}{6}= \frac{-2\pm\sqrt{-8}}{6}\\&= \frac{-2\pm 2i\sqrt{2}}{6}= \frac{-1\pm i\sqrt{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}\]


Answer   \(x=\dfrac{-1\pm i\sqrt{2}}{3}\)

q: Let \( z_1=2-i \) and \( z_2=1+3i \). Find \( \dfrac{z_1 z_2}{\bar{z}_2} \) in the form \( a+bi \).
Express \( z=\dfrac{(1-i)^2}{1+i} \) in trigonometric form with \( -\pi<\theta\le\pi \).
c:
Solution

Simplify the expression first.

\[\begin{aligned}(1-i)^2&=1-2i+i^2=-2i,\\z&=\frac{-2i}{1+i}=\frac{-2i(1-i)}{(1+i)(1-i)}=\frac{-2i+2i^2}{2}\\&= -i+i^2=-1-i.\end{aligned}\]


Now \( r=\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt{2} \). Since \( \cos\theta=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \) and \( \sin\theta=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \), we have \( \theta=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).

\(z=\sqrt{2}\Bigl(\cos\Bigl(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\Bigr)+i\sin\Bigl(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\Bigr)\Bigr).\)


Answer   \(\sqrt{2}\Bigl(\cos\Bigl(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\Bigr)+i\sin\Bigl(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\Bigr)\Bigr)\)

q: If \( z=-1+\sqrt{3}\, i \), find \( z^3 \) using De Moivre's theorem.
c:
Solution

Convert to trigonometric form:

\[\begin{aligned}r&=\sqrt{(-1)^2+(\sqrt{3})^2}=2,\\\cos\theta&=-\frac12,\quad\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\implies\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}.\end{aligned}\]


\(z=2\Bigl(\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}\Bigr).\)


By De Moivre's theorem,

\[\begin{aligned}z^3&=2^3\Bigl(\cos 2\pi+i\sin 2\pi\Bigr)=8(1+0i)=8.\end{aligned}\]


Answer   \(8\)

q: Find the cube roots of \( -8 \) in trigonometric form.
c:
Solution

Write \( -8=8(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi) \). The cube roots are

\(w_k=2\left(\cos\frac{\pi+2k\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{\pi+2k\pi}{3}\right),\quad k=0,1,2.\)


\[\begin{aligned}k=0:\quad &2\Bigl(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\Bigr),\\k=1:\quad &2(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi),\\k=2:\quad &2\Bigl(\cos\frac{5\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{5\pi}{3}\Bigr).\end{aligned}\]


Answer   \( 2\bigl(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr) \), \( 2(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi) \), \( 2\bigl(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\bigr) \)

q: Find the square roots of \( z=4\bigl(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\bigr) \) in trigonometric form.

c:
Solution

By De Moivre's theorem, \( z^n=\cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta) \).

Also \( \dfrac{1}{z^n}=z^{-n}=\cos(n\theta)-i\sin(n\theta) \).

Subtracting,

\[\begin{aligned}z^n-\frac{1}{z^n}&= \bigl(\cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta)\bigr)-\bigl(\cos(n\theta)-i\sin(n\theta)\bigr)\\&= 2i\sin(n\theta).\end{aligned}\]


Answer   shown

Solution

We have \( 1+i\sqrt{3}=2\bigl(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr) \) and \( 1-i\sqrt{3}=2\bigl(\cos\bigl(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr)+i\sin\bigl(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr)\bigr) \).

\[\begin{aligned}(1+i\sqrt{3})^4&= 2^4\Bigl(\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}\Bigr)= 16\Bigl(-\frac12-i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\Bigr)\\&= -8-8i\sqrt{3},\\(1-i\sqrt{3})^4&= 16\Bigl(\cos\Bigl(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\Bigr)+i\sin\Bigl(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\Bigr)\Bigr)\\&= -8+8i\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}\]


Adding these gives

\((-8-8i\sqrt{3})+(-8+8i\sqrt{3})=-16.\)


Answer   \(-16\)

q: Find a quadratic equation with real coefficients that has \( 1+2i \) as a root.
c:
Solution

Real coefficients force complex roots to occur in conjugate pairs, so the other root is \( 1-2i \).

\[\begin{aligned}\text{sum}&=(1+2i)+(1-2i)=2,\\\text{product}&=(1+2i)(1-2i)=1+4=5.\end{aligned}\]


The monic equation is \( x^2-(\text{sum})x+(\text{product})=0 \), that is

\(x^2-2x+5=0.\)


Answer   \(x^2-2x+5=0\)

By De Moivre's theorem,

\[\begin{aligned}z^4&=(\sqrt{2})^4\bigl(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi\bigr)=4(-1)=-4,\\z^{-2}&=(\sqrt{2})^{-2}\Bigl(\cos\Bigl(-\frac{\pi}{2}\Bigr)+i\sin\Bigl(-\frac{\pi}{2}\Bigr)\Bigr)\\&= \frac12\bigl(0-i\bigr)=-\frac{i}{2}.\end{aligned}\]


Answer   \( z^4=-4 \), \( \dfrac{1}{z^2}=-\dfrac{i}{2} \)

q: Show that \( \overline{z_1 z_2}=\bar{z}_1\bar{z}_2 \) for \( z_1=3+i \) and \( z_2=2-5i \).
c:
Solution

The product and its conjugate:

\[\begin{aligned}z_1 z_2&=(3+i)(2-5i)=6-15i+2i-5i^2=11-13i,\\\overline{z_1 z_2}&=11+13i.\end{aligned}\]


On the other side,

\[\begin{aligned}\bar{z}_1=3-i,\quad\bar{z}_2=2+5i,\\\bar{z}_1\bar{z}_2&=(3-i)(2+5i)=6+15i-2i-5i^2=11+13i.\end{aligned}\]


Therefore \( \overline{z_1 z_2}=\bar{z}_1\bar{z}_2 \).

Answer   shown
